https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Many migrants have attempted to swim from Morocco to the Spanish enclave Ceuta By Marianna Spring Social media investigations correspondent and Top Comment host Published 6 hours ago This weekend, Mohammed wants to travel from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta, on the northern tip of Africa. He's a Moroccan man in his twenties and wants to emigrate to Europe - not least because he's been seeing lots of videos on Instagram that make the trip look easy. He contacts several of the Instagram accounts and one replies, claiming to have helped "many people" and offering him advice on how to cross for hundreds of pounds. Except Mohammed isn't real - he's a dummy account I've set up to investigate a network of interconnected Instagram profiles that are driving the influx of migrants to Ceuta with aspirational content and offering them help for a fee. It comes after roughly 78,000 migrants from Morocco arrived by sea into Ceuta in a matter of hours last month, 100 of whom died according to the Mayor of Ceuta. The crisis has calmed since, but it has sparked tensions between EU nations who share open borders as well as criticism of the Spanish government. The BBC's Top Comment podcast has identified dozens of Instagram profiles that portray the short swim around the Morocco-Ceuta border fence as safe and easy - but in reality, people have drowned trying to make the crossing and take much longer routes. The accounts also wrongly show Ceuta as a viable route to mainland Europe. Our research suggests that this has contributed to the influx, alongside other factors such as misinformation about changes to Spanish immigration law and allegations about weak border controls. 'Help you enter Ceuta' After engaging with the accounts' profiles and posts, the BBC was added to multiple channels and WhatsApp groups. When I asked one of the anonymous accounts if they could help me cross to Ceuta this weekend, they said yes and requested "5000 dirhams upfront" (Â£400) for "information that will help you enter Ceuta". They said they had helped "many people" cross before and would give me information about the "sewer pipes" which I could use to help me reach the enclave safely. The account confirmed lots of other Instagram profiles help people to cross to Ceuta in this way, and asked for payment "via bank account" with a specific money transfer service. But they didn't respond when asked whether I would get a refund if the crossing was not successful. They've since deleted several of their messages to the account. Image caption, The network of Instagram accounts make the trip seem easy Image caption, Part of the exchange between our dummy account and one of the accounts, under a pseudonym, claiming to help Moroccan migrants reach Ceuta The same profile giving this advice had previously told my real, BBC Instagram account that "it does not encourage immigration to Ceuta" - a message several other profiles repeated. And it's continuing - social media posts, actively recommended by Instagram's algorithm, are advertising another attempt at the crossing this weekend. This risks further deaths and inflamed diplomatic tensions between Morocco and Spain. Several of the profiles are no longer on Instagram after the BBC contacted Meta, which owns the platform. Meta told the BBC: "We have a team monitoring the situation in Ceuta in real time and removing content that violates our policies - including content that offers to provide, facilitate or seek human smuggling services". Why the network matters I first noticed the deluge of content about Ceuta when I saw a viral video showing two women in wetsuits walking through the city. While the original post in Spanish sought to dissuade migrants from arriving in Ceuta with the caption "Ceuta can't take it anymore", some versions shared by Moroccan and Arabic-speaking accounts either changed the caption or cropped it out, so the clip only showed the women strolling freely. This was just one of hundreds of posts that we are calling "mirage" content, which paint a deceptive picture of a place distinct from reality. Some videos show groups of young men and women swimming happily in the sea - even though many have drowned making the trip in recent weeks. Others show stories of people who have succeeded in reaching Ceuta - and then claim they have gone on to reach Spain or mainland Europe, despite about 75,000 of the 78,000 arrivals having been returned to Morocco by authorities. Exposed: the faceless accounts inflaming the Ceuta crisis Top Comment Listen on Sounds There were lots of similarities in the profiles sharing this kind of content. Nearly 40 of them had variations of the term Haraga and include Ceuta in their name or handle, often with a Spanish flag as a profile picture and with the calling codes for Morocco and Spain in the description. Haraga in Maghrebi Arabic roughly translates to "those who burn" and is used colloquially to refer to migrants arriving in a new place and burning or destroying documents so they cannot be identified and deported back to their home countries. The account history of these profiles, coupled with their posts and followers, indicated that most were being run from Morocco while a few were potentially based in Spain or Italy. Lots of them had been set up several years before, but their content about Ceuta had gained more traction in recent weeks. Image caption, The accounts are gaming the algorithm with aspirational videos of Ceuta The accounts have managed to manipulate the algorithms on major social media sites by sharing emotive and hopeful content to gain more traction. Insiders at the biggest social media companies have previously told me how posts triggering a strong reaction are more likely to go viral. When I tried to contact some of these profiles using my own account, some of them directed me to the same WhatsApp numbers or email addresses. My dummy account, Mohammed, was a profile set to private and designed to look similar to the accounts of younger Moroccan people who were liking and commenting on the posts advertising crossings. I followed relevant content, including several of the Haraga profiles, and soon my feed was swamped with videos and content encouraging travel to Ceuta. There appears to be a wider trend here, where people looking to charge migrants money for advice can easily set up profiles and game social media algorithms. While there have been Facebook groups and accounts on other major social media sites posting about Ceuta, it was on Instagram where I found the most active and prevalent group of interconnected accounts. The new-found reach of these profiles, facilitated by Instagram's algorithms, opens them up to a wider pool of paying clients. It is yet another example of how gaming an algorithm can fuel real-world harm. Photograph: Dnipropetrovk regional military administration/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Firefighters at work at the shopping mall hit in the deadly Russian drone attack in Kryvyi Rih, central Ukraine. Photograph: Dnipropetrovk regional military administration/AFP/Getty Images Ukraine Attack on Ukraine shopping centre that killed 16 is ‘terror by design’, says EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, threatens harshest sanctions yet on Russia after strike on Kryvyi Rih, the home town of Volodymyr Zelenskyy Agence France-Presse Fri 21 Aug 2026 21.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian drones have slammed into a busy shopping centre in central Ukraine , killing 16 people in an attack that Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned as “cynical and despicable”. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, condemned Friday’s attack on Kryvyi Rih – the president’s home town – as “terror by design” and said she was “putting forward the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war” when ministers meet in Ireland next month. “Russia’s attack against a shopping centre in [Kryvyi Rih] shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow’s war,” Kallas said on X, claiming that Moscow “wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable”. Ukrainian publishers call for support after Russian attacks destroy 10m books Read more The strike comes as Russia has intensified its bombardments of Ukrainian cities in recent months. Separately, four more people, including three children, were killed in another strike in the southern Mykolaiv region, the interior minister, Ivan Vygivsky, said on Telegram. Videos on social media of the Kryvyi Rih attack showed rescuers rushing to help the wounded on the street outside, as smoke poured out of the building. A second drone smashed into the roof of the building about half an hour after the first – a repeat strike that Zelenskyy said in a post on X was “targeting the emergency responders”. Ukrainian emergency services initially said the attack had killed 15 people and wounded 130 others, 23 of them children. The head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, Oleksandr Ganzha, later said on Telegram the death toll had risen to 16. In his X post, Zelenskyy condemned “an absolutely cynical and despicable strike ... carried out by the Russians against an ordinary shopping centre”. View image in fullscreen The shopping centre in the aftermath of the Russian attack. Photograph: Prosecutor general’s office/Telegram/Reuters Kryvyi Rih, an industrial city about 60km (37 miles) from the front line, has come under repeated Russian attacks throughout the war. Ukraine’s allies are to meet on Monday to reaffirm their support for Kyiv in talks held on the country’s independence day. The meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” will be co-chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. About 10 leaders including the European Council chief, António Costa, will be in Kyiv for the coalition meeting, according to an EU official. Zelenskyy urged a strong response from Ukraine’s allies. “The world must respond to them accordingly – with real pressure on the aggressor. For peace to be possible, Russia must face real accountability,” he said. Zelenskyy held a call with the UN chief, António Guterres, on Friday, updating him on Russian strikes and the civilian casualties they had caused, the Ukrainian leader said on X. Kyiv has repeatedly appealed to its allies for additional support as Russia steps up its strikes, with Ukrainian forces struggling in particular to intercept salvos of ballistic missiles. https://www.dw.com/en/us-strikes-oil-tan.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MI7e The US Central Command shared footage of the strikes on Iranian shops Image: U.S. Central Command/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement The US military struck five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it struck the ships "after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days." "The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it added. CENTCOM said it directed the crews to abandon ship shortly before the strikes. The were no immediate reports regarding casualties. Iranian media reported explosions were heard near the southern port of Jask and on Kharg Island — both key ports for the country's oil exports . What do we know about the ships that were attacked? US forces attacked four Iranian oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman: the M/T Kaviz, the M/T Charminar, the M/T Horizon 1 and the M/T Riesco. US forces also attacked the M/T Derya near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz . CENTCOM linked these five vessels to the IRGC. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement. "Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels." Iran announces retaliation Iranian state media reported that Iran launched missiles toward US targets in Jordan. Jordan's army said Wednesday it shot down 18 missiles from Iran. Jordan is a US ally and hosts an American military facilty. "Jordan's air defense systems engaged 20 ballistic missiles launched toward Jordanian territory, successfully intercepting and destroying 18 of them, while two missiles fell in unpopulated areas," the army statement said, adding that Iran fired the missiles. Early on Wednesday morning, the IRCG also said it would target oil tankers off the coast of Bahrain and Kuwait in retaliation for the US strikes. "We warn all oil tankers in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports... whether they are anchored or docked — we warn them to leave their vessels because they will be targeted," the IRCG said in a statement. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Search and rescue operations in the rubble of the collapsed multi-storey building in Gaza City. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Search and rescue operations in the rubble of the collapsed multi-storey building in Gaza City. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Gaza At least 12 killed after building in Gaza City damaged by Israeli strikes collapses Rescue workers say search for about 100 people, including 50 children, hampered by lack of heavy machinery Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem, Seham Tantesh in Gaza and agencies Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.10 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A building housing displaced Palestinian families collapsed on Wednesday in Gaza City, killing at least 12 people, as rescuers searched the rubble for about 100 people including 50 children believed to be trapped. A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 14 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them. The bombed-out multi storey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way, it fell on to tents housing displaced families beside it, witnesses said. View image in fullscreen Rescue workers remove the body of a victim from the collapsed building in south-western Gaza City. Photograph: Hamza Z H Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty Images The collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza. Mohammed Abu Dan, a superviser with the civil defence team recovering victims, said more than 10 families had been living in the building and displaced people had been forced to stay there because no other shelter was available. US set to deliver 2,000lb bombs to Israel as part of vast arms deal Read more “Search and rescue operations are being carried out under extremely difficult conditions due to a lack of the necessary equipment and resources,” Abu Dan said. Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its restrictions are intended to prevent equipment from reaching militant groups. A video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza’s civil defence spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a young girl wrapped in a bloodstained scarf. Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defence service, said: “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people.” Alessandro Mrakic, the head of the UN Development Programme’s Gaza office, said rescuers from UN agencies were taking part in the operation, which he described as extremely difficult because of the lack of appropriate machinery. Egypt’s relief agency was also involved. “There are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare [for more deaths],” Mrakic said. Tents belonging to displaced families had been erected along the road beside the building because there was nowhere else for them to shelter. View image in fullscreen The search for survivors and the dead in the rubble continued on Wednesday. Photograph: Hamza Z. H. Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty Images Similar incidents have occurred repeatedly over the past two years, with dozens of homes and buildings damaged during the war later collapsing, trapping people and causing further deaths and injuries. With few other options, many Palestinians have returned to partly destroyed homes or moved into abandoned buildings, clearing small spaces among the rubble despite the danger. Soaring rents and the cost of vacant land have made finding safer accommodation increasingly difficult. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians also remain unable to return to neighbourhoods near the so-called yellow line , forcing families to find whatever space they can elsewhere. In May, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to seize 70% of Gaza . Damaged roofs, walls and supporting columns can collapse without warning, particularly during strong winds, heavy rain or further bombardment. Asked whether they feared for themselves and their children, people living there said: “Yes, we are afraid, but where can we go? This is better than staying out on the street.” Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. View image in fullscreen Civil defence and municipal teams conduct search and rescue operations. Photograph: Saeed M M T Jaras/Anadolu/Getty Images This year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza . Separately, a video from the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of Gaza City showed the aftermath of an Israeli drone strike that killed Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded several other people. Al-Zinati had been trying to recover the body of a man killed in an earlier strike. Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumed full-scale war in Gaza and moved to force out its Palestinian population. Katz, responding to criticism from another rightwing politician before the 27 October elections, said 70% of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s offensive launched after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. He added that the Israel Defense Forces was prepared “to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan”,. Since the war began, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: Air France has reportedly said that it will follow Israel's new rules restricting pilots and cabin crew members holding the nationality, including dual nationality, of countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel from operating flights to or over the country.The restrictions reportedly cover nationals of 31 countries, including Pakistan, Iran, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia and Algeria, according to Al Jazeera, which cited Israeli media reports and French investigative publication Mediapart.The policy has raised concerns over the treatment of airline employees based on their nationality and the challenges it could create for international carriers operating services to Israel.“Like all airlines, Air France is required to comply with the entry regulations established by the authorities of the countries it serves, both for its customers and employees,” Al Jazeera quoted the airline as saying. An internal memo to Air France pilots and cabin crew, reviewed by Mediapart, reportedly warned that non-compliance could expose both the airline and the employee concerned to sanctions.What are Israel's new restrictions on airline crew?Israel's Ministry of Transport and Road Safety informed foreign airlines on October 1 that pilots and cabin crew operating flights into Israeli airspace must not hold the nationality, including dual nationality, of countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, according to Israeli broadcaster N12.The restrictions reportedly apply to citizens of 31 countries. However, an internal United Airlines scheduling memo listed 29 countries, according to reports.Apart from Pakistan, Iran, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Indonesia and Malaysia, the affected countries reportedly include Afghanistan, Iraq, Lebanon, Qatar, Syria and Yemen, among others.The directive could require international airlines employing crew members from these countries to revise staffing arrangements for flights to Israel.Flydubai incident reported a day before restrictionsThe restrictions were reportedly reinforced following an incident involving a Flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30.According to Al Jazeera, citing Emirati and Israeli authorities, an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the Indian captain and attempted to hijack the aircraft. The co-pilot was also accused of trying to crash the plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport.The Indian captain was reportedly injured and has been recovering in hospital.Israel issued the directive the following day. However, the precise connection between the incident and the introduction of the restrictions has not been independently established in the available reports.Which other airlines are complying with Israel's rules?Air France is among the airlines that have addressed the restrictions. Smartwings, the Czech Republic's largest airline, also confirmed receiving the instructions and said it would comply with the applicable requirements.“We received the directive from the Israeli authorities in September 2026. We have carefully reviewed the directive and continue to monitor and comply with all applicable requirements issued by the relevant authorities,” Vladimira Dufkova, a Smartwings spokesperson, told Al Jazeera.The airline said the directive had not affected its operations, crew management procedures or the deployment of crew members on flights to and from Israel.United Airlines has also informed pilots and cabin crew about nationality-based restrictions, according to reports. However, the US carrier declined to provide further details to Al Jazeera and did not confirm whether it had received the Israeli directive or taken action in response.
